 Oral Judgment :
1. The respondent No.2 being dead, the appeal abates against him.

2. This appeal challenges the legality and correctness of the judgment and order dated 10th October,
2002, rendered in Regular Criminal Case No.34/1996, by the Judicial Magistrate, First Class,
Buldhana, acquitting the respondents of the offence punishable under Section 7(i) read with Section 16(1)(a)(ii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (hereinafter referred to as, "the PFA Act").

The respondent No.1 and deceased respondent No.2 were charged with an offence of selling and storing under the brand name "WONDER Biscuits"
which were adulterated and did not conform to the food standard prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules framed thereunder.
The non- conformity was in the nature of presence of acidic extracted fat beyond the prescribed limit.
3. The sample of the biscuits was taken at about 2.00 p.m. of 11.2.1994 from the shop of respondent No.1, situated at village Raipur, District Buldhana.

It was stated in the complaint that the sample so taken weighed 1 Kg. and it was divided into three parts, one of which was sent to public analyst,
Pune for analysis and report and remaining two samples were handed over in a sealed condition to the Local Health Authority, Buldhana.
Needless to say, the sample that was obtained was after payment of its price to the respondent No.1.

The report of Public Analysis, Pune was adverse and it stated that the sample that was subjected to analysis was adulterated and did not conform to the Food Standard prescribed under PFA Act and the Rules framed thereunder.
Therefore, it was also alleged that these biscuits were manufactured and sold by respondent No.2 to respondent No.1 who in turn stored them for sale and also sold to the complainant.
There was no specific allegations made against the respondent Nos.3 and 4.

Accordingly, a complaint was filed against all the respondents and they were prosecuted for the offence punishable under Section 7(i) read with Section 16(1)(a)(ii)
of the PFA Act.

4. On merits of the case, the learned Magistrate found that the complainant failed to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt against all the respondents and, therefore, acquitted them of the offence State Of Maharashtra vs Mr.Eknath Gopal Lokhande Kirana Dukan ... on 14 February, 2018 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/28693663/

sentences.text: Not being satisfied with the same, the appellant-State is before this Court in the present appeal.

5. I have heard Shri P.S. Tembhare, learned Additional Public Prosecutor for the appellant, Shri P.B.
Patil, learned counsel for respondent No.1 and Shri S.A. Mohta, learned counsel for respondent No.4.
Nobody is present on behalf of respondent Nos.2 & 3.
I have carefully gone through the record of the case and the impugned judgment and order.

6. In this case, admittedly, there was no charge framed against the respondent Nos.3 and 4 and,
therefore, one does not understand as to why they were made to stand the trial.
Nevertheless, by their acquittal in this case, no prejudice having been caused to them, I do not wish to make any further comments on the mistake committed by the trial Court in this case.

7. It is seen that the respondent No.1 and deceased respondent No.2 admitted that the biscuits in question were manufactured and sold by respondent No.2 to respondent No.1 and respondent No.1 in turn stored them for sale and sold them to the Food Inspector, the complainant.

These admissions would narrow down the controversy involved in the appeal to the question of following of the mandatory procedure prescribed under various Rules framed under the provisions of the PFA Act.

8. On going through these record of the case as well as the impugned judgment and order, I find that a few mandatory provisions of law, Rule 12, 14 to 16 of the PFA Rules, have not been followed by the complainant.
Rule 12 requires written notice to be issued in form No.VI about proposed procurement of sample by following the procedure under Section 11(1)(a) of the PFA Act.

The evidence on record shows that this procedure has not been followed and the learned Magistrate has made a detailed discussion about non-compliance of this procedure in paragraphs 15 and 16 of the impugned judgment and order.
I do not find any perversity in the conclusion made by the learned Magistrate about not following of the procedure of Rule 12 of the PFA Rules.
9. It is further seen that as required under Rule 14 to 16
, a detailed procedure for sealing of the samples has necessarily to be followed by the Food Inspector.
It is also necessary for the Food Inspector to give evidence before the Court about the details of such procedure.

If he fails to mention the details of the sealing procedure adopted by him, a room is created to doubt the integrity of the samples and possibility of they being either tampered with or influenced adversely by weather conditions is not ruled out.
These rules have been held to be mandatory by this Court in many of its judgments, some of which have been relied upon by the trial Court.
These judgments are in the cases of Kundal vs. Shivpur Warwade Municipality, reported in 1986 Cr. L.J. 931 Bombay and Rameshran vs. State of Maharashtra, reported in 1983 Cri. L.J. 125 Bombay.

sentences.text: However, no such evidence giving details as to how the samples were sealed by the Food Inspector was tendered by him.

That was the reason why the learned Magistrate has found that there is violation with mandatory provisions of law resulting from non-following of the procedure prescribed under Rules 14 to 16 of the PFA Rules,
the benefit of which must go to the accused persons, and rightly so.
